extracted.intended_audience: NIH grant applicants, program analysts, and people who analyze/track NIH peer review and funding patterns (especially NIDA applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing NIH (and IC-specific) R01-equivalent funding and review percentile distributions to detect deviations from an expected uniform spread, infer reviewer behavior relative to perceived paylines, and quantify over/under-representation of scored applications across percentile bins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use NIH RePORT / Data Book R01-eqv percentile data
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIH Data Book / RePORT section allows checking R01-equivalent funding by percentile rank for each completed fiscal year from 2014 onward, for all of NIH or for each IC with funding authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these official per-FY percentile breakdowns as the primary data source; they reveal IC virtual paylines and anomalous funding at poor percentiles. This is the starting dataset for any analysis of percentile/funding patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collapse percentile bins and convert to percent of scored applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Collapsing across two percentile bins (e.g., combine 1st and 2nd percentile into a single bar) and converting the number of applications in each combined bin to a percent of the scored applications (not all assigned applications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggregating small bins reduces noise when counts per bin are low. Compute percent-of-scored-applications to compare observed proportions to an expected uniform distribution; plotting a horizontal expected-value line (see next metric) helps visualize deviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected uniform distribution null: ~4% per 2%-ile bin
rubrics_metrics.description: If scoring were evenly distributed across scored applications, approximately 4% of the scored applications would fall into each 2%-ile bin (since 100%/50 bins ≈ 2% bins → 4% per combined 2%-ile grouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this as a simple null hypothesis for detecting over- or under-representation in particular percentile ranges. Draw a line at the expected 4% when plotting to see where bins exceed or fall short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose correct denominator — use only scored applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The data cutoff often occurs around the mid-50s because roughly half of proposals are not scored and are placed into the 50+ bin; therefore denominator should be the number of scored applications when assessing distribution across percentiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not include unscored/triaged applications in the denominator for per-percentile analyses, since that would distort expected proportions per scored bin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for triage and the roughness of the triage rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The triage process is only a rough rule of thumb and the bias is supposed to be toward more than 50% being unscored; this leads to some scores above the 50th percentile and unevenities around the 50% cutoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize triage's coarse nature when interpreting unexpected scored entries above 50th percentile; don't assume strict cutoff behavior, and annotate analyses with triage limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider scoring/tie-rule changes and their effect (ties at 20, 30, 40)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scoring was revised to produce many ties at overall impact scores of 20, 30 and 40, which makes it difficult to intuit the impact on resulting percentile distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in policy-driven scoring/rounding/tie effects when modeling expected distributions or when comparing across years with different scoring rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Percentile ranks may come from multiple study sections — aggregate with caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentile ranks reported for an application could be derived from competitions that involved grants assigned to multiple different ICs and different study sections may have very different score-to-percentile relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aggregating across ICs or NIH-wide, be cautious: heterogeneity across study sections can produce misleading overall patterns. Where possible, stratify analyses by study section or account for differing score-percentile calibrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for reviewer behavior relative to perceived payline (the 'wedge' effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer behavior may be sensitive to where reviewers believe the payline will be; panels may push more applications than expected below a perceived cut (e.g., 16th percentile) and push disliked applications upward, producing an overrepresentation at the top bins and underrepresentation in middle bins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test for over-representation in low-percentile bins and compensating under-representation in mid-percentile bins as evidence that reviewers are emphasizing a fund/do-not-fund line rather than uniformly scoring across the distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify over- and under-representation to estimate excess/deficit awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the difference between observed bin counts and expected counts (under the uniform null) to estimate how many grants have been given better or worse scores than expected by chance (e.g., author's example: ~44 extra in first two bins; ~136 up to 14th percentile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these counts to put a magnitude on the wedge effect and to compare across ICs or years. Report absolute counts and percentages to make implications for funding clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare IC-specific distributions to NIH-wide and across fiscal years
rubrics_metrics.description: Patterns observed for NIDA in FY2023 may mirror NIH-wide patterns across FY2014–2023, though the exact cutoff where overrepresentation appears varies by year (e.g., 14th percentile in FY2020).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check multiple fiscal years and compare IC-specific curves to the NIH aggregate to determine whether observed effects are idiosyncratic or systemic and whether cutoffs/time trends shift over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternate hypotheses for observed deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternate explanations include chance, or that the best grants in a given study section were disproportionately assigned to one IC (e.g., NIDA) while poorer grants went to others — both could produce similar over/under patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate assignment patterns, randomness, and cross-IC composition before concluding reviewer bias; run sensitivity analyses and null simulations where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear visualizations (stacked bars, collapsed bins) to reveal patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The NIGMS approach of using stacked bars is suggested as better for seeing distributions; collapsing to wider bins (e.g., 2%-ile groups) can make trends clearer when counts per bin are small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose visualization style appropriate to counts: stacked bars for composition, collapsed bins for trend clarity, and draw expected-value reference lines. Export tabular counts alongside plots for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't conflate scored percentile with funding outcome — note funding paylines
rubrics_metrics.description: Some grants were scored at high percentiles (e.g., 65th, 68th) but nothing was funded above a certain percentile (e.g., 48th), so scored percentiles and actual funding decisions interact with IC paylines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating fairness or reviewer behavior, always compare scoring distributions against actual funded-percentile cutoffs (virtual paylines) to see which scoring deviations had funding consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand opacity between post-discussion scores and the voted overall impact score
rubrics_metrics.description: The voted overall impact score sits somewhere between the post-discussion scores and panel members generally do not know what it will be; assigned reviewers only provide a rough post-discussion score window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for this scoring uncertainty and measurement noise when interpreting post-discussion scores and their translation into percentiles; avoid over-precision in attributing motives to small score shifts.
